The stock market just might shuffle to a weekly win, helped by all those good vibes around the energy sector, small caps and the royal wedding.
Itll be close though, as China and North Korea remain headaches, and the 10-year Treasury yield remains a big problem. Some traders, of course, a Immersion Beats, Guides Higher – The Apple Settlement Leads To A Long Tail On Revenues
Immersion Corporation (NASDAQ:IMMR) reported stronger than expected revenues for Q1 2018 and guided higher for the full year.
Cash and cash equivalents increased $92.5 million in the quarter, mostly as a result of the recent Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) settlement.
Management now expects revenues in 2018 to range between $108 million and $118 million, independent of possible litigation outcomes.
At the midpoint of guidance, there is little doubt that 2018 represents an inflection point in the recent story of the company:
Author chart, historical data from company’s filings, 2018 estimates are our own speculation based on Immersion’s midpoint of guidance
Fixed license fee contracts leading to strong revenue fluctuations due to their timing of execution
The recent adoption of the new ASC 606 standard for revenue recognition has certainly caused a strong impact on Q1 revenues, mostly due to the execution of the Apple license.
However, company’s guidance indicates that, even absent any new substantial contract or settlement, a decent revenue stream should be recorded in the next three quarters, too, due to variable (per unit) revenues and what the company describes as “Performance obligation B” for fixed license contracts:
In applying ASC 606, the Company is required to recognize revenue from a fixed fee license agreement when it has satisfied its performance obligations the Company has concluded that it has two separate performance obligations:
Performance Obligation A: to transfer rights to the Company’s patent portfolio as it exists when the contract is executed;
Performance Obligation B: to transfer rights to the Company’s patent portfolio as it evolves over the term of the contract, including access to new patent applications that the licensee can benefit from over the term of the contract.
Source: 10Q 2018, pg. 7
While performance A will represent a majority of recorded revenues, performance B may still have a significant impact especially for long term contracts like the Apple settlement, as we will soon discuss.
Here is a quick look at how revenues may look like in the next three quarters according to IMMR guidance:
Author chart, estimates based on IMMR midpoint of guidance. Q4 estimated higher due to seasonality. Possible litigation outcomes excluded from guidance.
Investors will continue to experience unpredictable lumpiness in Immersion’s reported revenues, but it is key for investors to try to decipher the underneath “predictable” revenue trend to get a sense of the long term sustainability of the business model.
The Apple settlement: some additional speculations
There is little doubt that most of IMMR Q1 2018 revenues derive from the Apple settlement, with some positive impact coming also from the renewal of a few contracts in the automotive vertical.
However, the Apple contract will also have a “long tail” impact on IMMR future revenues, in a similar way to the Nintendo long term agreement.
Here is a key part in Immersion’s most recent 10-Q that allows for some speculation about the length and impact of the Apple settlement on future revenues:
Contracted revenue
Based on contracts signed and payments received as of March 31, 2018, the Company expects to recognize $38.6 million revenue related to Performance Obligation B under its fixed fee license agreements, which is satisfied over time, including $14.3 million over one to three years, and $24.3 million over more than three years, respectively.
Source: 10Q 2018, pg. 10 – emphasis added
We assume most of these contracted revenues derive from Apple and Nintendo. We previously estimated a $1 million per quarter, 6 year contract for Nintendo (OTCPK:NTDOF) (NTDOY) that will expire in Q3 2022.
We speculate the Apple contract may be slightly longer that the Nintendo one, with an option that allows Apple to renew until the expiration of Immersion’s licensed patents:
If Apple exercises the Option and pays the Option Fee to Immersion in accordance with Section 3.2, then this Agreement shall continue until the expiration of the last Immersion Patent.
Source: 10Q 2018, pg. 6 of the CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT AND LICENSE AGREEMENT BETWEEN IMMERSION AND APPLE
Samsung litigation coming to some key deadlines in court
The next big settlement in the mobility vertical may come from Samsung, a long term partner of the company, contributing roughly $20 million per year in revenues, that didn’t renew its contract in 2015.
While it is impossible to predict if and when a settlement could come, we notice that Immersion’s court strategy is putting some short term pressure on Samsung in China, where the trial seems to be getting close to some key events:
Immersion Corporation vs. Samsung (China) Investment Co., Ltd., Huizhou Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd and Fujian Province Min Xin Household Electrical Appliances Technology Service Co., Ltd. (Fuzhou Intellectual Property Court – Case: Min 01 Min Chu No. 342 (2018)
A pretrial conference is scheduled for June 14-15, 2018. Samsung China and Samsung Huizhou filed Petitions for Invalidation on April 16, 2018 with the Chinese Patent Office (“SIPO”) for all three patents. Samsung China and Samsung Huizhou may supplement their petitions by May 16, 2018, and our response is due June 1, 2018.
Source: 10Q 2018, pg. 35
Good and bad news from the automotive and gaming sector, respectively
Automotive delivered record revenues of $6.8 million in Q1 2018, compared to $5.25 million for the whole of 2017.
While we should notice that there could be an “ASC 606 Performance A” impact on Q1 numbers, in a similar way to Apple, these numbers certainly bode well for IMMR future per-unit revenue stream.
In addition, we notice that most key suppliers to the automotive sector now seem to have signed a license with the company. Unlike in the mobility vertical, we expect very little litigation necessary in this vertical.
On the negative side, and due to the expiration of key patents in 2016 and the resulting lack of Sony as a customer, we notice that gaming is on a declining trend.
Conclusion
With Q1 2018 results now disclosed, investors may finally be able to get a better picture of IMMR revenue potential, navigating through some of the gimmicks caused by the new revenue recognition standard and the strict confidentiality of the Apple settlement.
The continued, positive reaction recorded by the share price after earnings may indicate that the market is slowly putting together some pieces of this complicated puzzle and valuing positively the developments in the mobility and automotive sector.
